author: Ansley Franco
title: Chatham County arrests have led to 124 people released to ICE custody in first seven months - NewsBreak
text:
By Ansley Franco ,
1 days ago
Even before the recent raid at Hyundai's Bryan County megasite that led to the arrest of 475 people, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) had already detained more than three times as many people in Chatham County this year than in all of 2024.
In the first seven months of President Donald Trump’s administration, ICE detained 124 people in the county — compared to just 35 during the entire previous year, according to government data. Of those detained in 2024, 22 have since been deported to countries including Mexico, Guatemala and Honduras.
Tawana Garrett, public information officer for the Chatham County Sheriff's office, told the Savannah Morning News that as of Sept. 10, the county detention center was currently holding 64 people for ICE.
Of the 124 people who have been placed in immigration hold this year from Chatham County, 65 have been removed from the country per the data provided by ICE in response to a Freedom of Information Act request to the Deportation Data Project and analyzed by the Savannah Morning News .
ICE’s Online Detainee Locator System shows there are five people who were arrested in Effingham County who are currently being held in an ICE detention center. Three are held in centers in Georgia, one is in Texas while the other is in California.
The Savannah-area is not unique in its increase of ICE agents' presence. Trump campaigned on a promise of stricter immigration guidelines, and has since signed an executive order that expanded ICE’s power , halted the processing of migrants and asylum seekers, and deported migrants.
Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Kristi Noem touted in her first 200 days on the job, 1.6 million “illegal immigrants have left the United States population,” — a statement based on preliminary estimates published by the Center for Immigration Studies .
And between Trump’s inauguration on Jan. 20 and July 31, ICE had arrested 4,500 undocumented immigrants in Georgia — a 367% increase of arrests compared to arrests in the same period in 2021, according to the DHS .
“ICE is once again empowered to remove the worst of the worst — including murderers, pedophiles, gang members, drug traffickers, and terrorists,” said a press release published by DHS on Aug. 20.
However, two-thirds of the 120,000 people arrested by ICE between January and May have no criminal history, according to data compiled by the Marshall Project , a nonprofit news organization.
And, the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER), an American private nonprofit research organization, found that relative to U.S.-born citizens, immigrants as a group have had lower incarceration rates for 150 years.
NBER also found immigrant's are 60% less likely to be incarcerated since 1960.
There are cases of undocumented immigrants committing violent crimes against others like the murder of Augusta University student Laken Riley in Athens last fall. But Daniela Rodriguez, director of Migrant Equity Southeast, a Savannah non-profit, said the small group of violent offenders should in no way represent the perception of all immigrants.
The government data reviewed by the Savannah Morning News did not include the specific charges or names of the people in the Savannah-area who were arrested and placed in ICE custody — instead, they were listed as having “2 pending criminal charges” or as “1 convicted criminal.”
ICE's partnership with Georgia police department's On May 2024, Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp signed Bill 1105 into state law, requiring local police departments to cooperate with ICE and potentially contributing to the increase seen in Chatham County.
“They get ran through a system and if they’re here illegally, there’s a hold. We have to detain them until ICE comes and gets them,” Garrett with the sheriff's office said. The frequency in which detainees get transported to a detention center outside of Savannah depends on ICE’s schedule, she added.
Betsy Nolen, public information officer for the Chatham County Police Department, wrote in an emailed statement on June 26, "The Chatham County Police Department does not have a formal partnership with ICE."
But police records from June 11 revealed ICE agents rode shotgun with CCPD officers.
Shortly after 6 a.m., ICE detained eight people in two seperate stops on Quacco Road. One report said a truck was stopped for having obscured license tags on the truck and trailer. In the other case, a van was pulled over after failing to stop when leaving Regency Trailer Park.
The police report showed those who were arrested ranged from 20 to 50 years old. ICE took custody of both drivers and one passenger from the incidents, according to CCPD Chief Jeff Hadley. It is unknown where the three are now.
"If someone has an ICE order, hold, or warrant, we alert ICE and they respond. This is exactly the same procedure that is used if someone has any type of warrant issued by another city, county, state, or court. We detain the person – no matter who they are – until the agency with the warrant takes custody of them,"CCPD public information officer Nolen wrote.
"This is the extent of our agency’s involvement with ICE."
Hadley said in an email on Sept. 3 that this was the only time ICE agents rode in CCPD patrol vehicles.
"The Chatham County Police Department does not independently engage in proactive immigration enforcement. We do not knock on doors, show up at businesses, or ask someone for proof of residency," the email stated.
Nolen did not answer how the partnership between the two CCPD officers and ICE agents began, but said June 11 was the only day the two law enforcement agencies collaborated.
SPD’s public information officer, Neil Pentilla wrote in an email, “The Savannah Police Department does not actively participate in Immigration and Customs Enforcement actions within our jurisdiction.”
Latin American men dominate local ICE arrest data Nearly half of the 181 people arrested in Chatham County and detained by ICE between September 2023 and late July 2025 are from Mexico. Only one person is not from Latin America and has the "People's Republic of China" listed as their country of origin.
The Georgia Budget and Policy Institute , a non-profit organization based in Atlanta, found that the 1.3 million immigrants who reside in Georgia fill about 15% of all jobs in the state — mainly in the construction, agriculture and forestry industries.
The organization noted that deporting Georgian workers "will rob city and state coffers of nearly $929 million in tax revenue, making it more difficult to provide basic services to all residents, harming all workers and families in our state."
Information collected by the Deportation Data Project shows that of the 181 people arrested in Chatham County and released to ICE custody between Sept. 2023 and late July 2025, 169 were aged between 20 and 44 years old.
All but two are men, with one person's sex is listed as "unknown."
Ansley Franco is an intern with the Savannah Morning News, covering public safety and general assignments. You can reach her at AFranco@gannett.com.
